papers.title: Males of a suboscine bird (Ceratopipra mentalis) exhibit individual distinctiveness in their contact call
papers.abstract: The ability to discriminate among individual conspecifics may play a role in competition, mate selection, and other social interactions. Studies of individual distinctiveness in birds have traditionally focused on oscines, owing to the assumption that the less vocally complex suboscines would be incapable of producing individually distinct vocalizations. Nevertheless, while studies remain limited, a growing body of literature indicates that suboscines are capable of producing individually distinct vocalizations. Ceratopipra mentalis, the red-capped manakin, is a lekking suboscine and an important seed disperser. This study investigates whether individual distinctiveness in the whistle-peep vocalization, a contact call between males, of C. mentalis exists by recording males at multiple leks in Panama. Using flexible discriminant function analyses, we found individual distinctiveness in temporal and frequency traits of the whistle-peep call structure. We were able to classify individuals with 81.1% accuracy, comparable to other studies of suboscines. These results provide further evidence that the absence of song learning and less complex syrinxes in suboscines do not preclude individual distinctiveness in vocalizations. While studies focus on territorial species, here we found individual distinctiveness in a non-territorial lekking species. We argue for the need to examine the role of vocalizations in mate selection and male-male competition in these species with intense sexual selection. Lastly, our results suggest that acoustic monitoring may be a useful path forward to obtain a rapid assessment of male population abundance in C. mentalis and potentially other suboscine species, critical given predicted changes in species with climate change and other human-induced impacts.

papers.title: From Wandering Thoughts to Mental Stillness: A Minimal Computational Statistical-Mechanical Model of Driven Relaxation
papers.abstract: Reduced spontaneous thought during meditation is often described phenomenologically, but a mechanistic account should specify how a dynamical system can enter and persist in such a regime. Here we formulate a minimal statistical-mechanical model in which a dimensionless coordinate, q, represents a coarse-grained propensity for spontaneous-thought activity, and a slowly relaxing variable, r of t, represents the history-dependent effect of an attentional manipulation. The model combines a tilted double-well landscape with Langevin noise, allowing a high-q and a low-q dynamical regime to coexist. We numerically integrate the model under a controlled focusing protocol followed by removal of the drive and quantify low-state occupancy, first-passage times, dwell times, occupancy entropy, and transition entropy. For the chosen dimensionless parameterization, increasing the drive amplitude produces a sharp crossover in low-state occupancy near the deterministic spinodal threshold, A-sub-sp, approximately equal to 0.0148. At a noise intensity of D equal to 0.01, the probability of occupying the low-q regime at drive removal increases from 0.094 at A equal to zero to 0.994 at A equal to 0.02, while the mean first-passage time decreases from 48.0 to 13.5 model time units. Noise produces a non-monotonic effect: for A equal to 0.01, low-state occupancy at drive removal is only 0.033 at D equal to 0.0025, rises to 0.842 at D equal to 0.02, and falls to 0.718 at D equal to 0.04. Strong driving also reduces the effective number of occupied states while changing transition entropy much less, illustrating why a single entropy measure cannot identify thoughtlessness. These results do not establish that human neural dynamics obey this model. Instead, they show that a driven stochastic bistable system can generate the qualitative sequence of focusing, switching, relaxation, and metastable low-activity residence, and they provide quantitative predictions that can be tested against time-resolved neural recordings and independent reports of subjective experience.

papers.title: Collateral effects of bacteriophage resistance on antibiotic sensitivity in Pseudomonas aeruginosa
papers.abstract: Collateral effect (CEs) of phage resistance can alter antibiotic sensitivity, leading to collateral sensitivity (CS). CS of phage resistance can potentially be used to design more effective phage--antibiotic combination treatments, yet insufficient knowledge on the occurrence of such phage resistance associated CS is currently available. Here, we characterized CEs across diverse Pseudomonas aeruginosa strains, antibiotics, and phages. For each of eight strains (seven clinical isolates and PAO1), we generated mutants resistant to phage PAO1-1 and, separately, mutants resistant to each of six antibiotics. Phage-resistant mutants were also generated using four additional phages (M32, NP1, NP3, and PNM), and double phage- and antibiotic-resistant mutants from one strain. We measured growth curves across antibiotic concentration ranges after which the area-under-the-curve (AUC) was quantified as a measure of bacterial burden. Dose-response curves for AUC against antibiotic concentrations were constructed to estimate a fold change in EC50 of mutants relative to their parental strains. PAO1-1-resistant mutants showed significant CS to colistin and polymyxin B. For other antibiotics, CEs varied by phage and parental strain: PAO1-1-resistant mutants showed CS to tobramycin, whereas mutants resistant to the other four phages tested were associated with CR. For double phage- and antibiotic resistant mutants we found CS to colistin and tobramycin relative to the parental strain. Resistance mutations occurred predominantly in genes involved in metabolism, virulence, and DNA replication. Antibiotic-resistant mutants also showed increased phage sensitivity, with the strongest effect in colistin-resistant mutants. In conclusion this study demonstrates collateral effects of phage resistance are most specific to both strain- and antibiotic-specific.

papers.title: PPARα genotype impacts bone quality and perfluorooctanoic acid-induced effects
papers.abstract: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are significant environmental contaminants that cause a number of adverse human health effects. Studies increasingly link exposure to PFAS with disruptions in osteoblast and osteoclast differentiation and function, reduced bone mineral density (BMD), and negative impacts on skeletal structure. In vivo studies on the effects of PFAS on bone health remain limited, with none investigating the impacts in mice expressing human peroxisome proliferator activated receptor (PPAR). Given PFASs ability to interact with the peroxisome proliferator activated receptor family and their importance in bone health, we present work investigating the effects of perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) exposure and PPAR genotype (mouse, human or null) on bone quality across two exposure periods (6 and 14 weeks) in mice fed a human relevant diet. In both exposure scenarios, the serum PFOA concentrations were {approx} 50 {micro}g/mL, similar to a highly exposed fluorochemical worker. We began by establishing the liver phenotype across exposures and genotypes. Across genotypes and exposure timing, PFOA increased liver to body weight ratios, but the contribution of increased triglycerides was reduced at 14 weeks. Exposure to PFOA increased hepatic PPAR-dependent gene expression (Acox) in both sexes and exposure periods, but only in mPPAR mice. The effect of PFOA on hepatic CAR- and PXR-dependent gene expression (Cyp2b10 and Cyp3a11, respectively) was more complex; with sex-, genotype-, and exposure timing-dependent differences. Trabecular and cortical bone parameters were not impacted by PFOA treatment, but genotype was a significant factor across sexes and exposure periods. mPPAR mice had higher trabecular tissue mineral density at 9 and 20 weeks of age than hPPAR mice, but the lower trabecular bone volume evident at 9 weeks of age resolved at 20 weeks of age. mPPAR mice had higher cortical tissue mineral density and bone volume than hPPAR and PPAR null mice. Analysis of serum markers of osteoblast and osteoclast activity following 14 weeks of exposure to PFOA revealed a PPAR-dependent decrease in PINP but no effect on CTX. Our results reveal the importance of PPAR genotype for bone quality parameters and emerging evidence of the effect of PFOA on osteoblast activity. Given the unusual mouse bone quality model (sv/129 background), this work underscores the need for future in vivo research shifts to investigate the effects of PFAS on in bone quality.

papers.title: 6-Methylnicotine is a strong agonist at α4β2 and α3β4 nicotinic cholinergic receptors
papers.abstract: (-)6-Methylnicotine (6-MN), is a structural analog of (-)nicotine that has been added to some e-cigarette/vape solutions and to nicotine oral pouches. 6-MN binds with high affinity to nicotinic cholinergic receptors (nAChRs) in brain, but its receptor subtype selectivity and its potency to activate and desensitize these receptors is unknown. Also unknown is whether chronic administration of 6-MN increases (upregulates) nAChRs in brain as does nicotine. Currently, 6-MN is unregulated in the U.S. by the FDA. Here we compared 6-MN and nicotine at 4{beta}2 and 3{beta}4 nAChRs, which are two major nAChR subtypes that mediate important functions in the brain and autonomic nervous system. Specifically, we quantitatively compared (-)6-MN and (-)nicotine with respect to receptor binding affinity and functional potency to activate 4{beta}2 and 3{beta}4 nAChRs, as well as its potency to desensitize these receptors, which is one of the key effects of nicotine. In addition, because chronic administration of nicotine upregulates the number of 4{beta}2 nAChRs in rat, mouse and human brain, we measured whether 6-MN also increases these receptors. Our results indicate that 6-MN is a more potent agonist than nicotine at both the 4{beta}2 and 3{beta}4 nAChRs, and it also upregulates nAChRs in brain.

papers.title: Green synthesis of silver nanoparticles from Artemisia afra and Artemisia annua leaf extracts: Enhanced in vitro anthelmintic activity against Haemonchus contortus
papers.abstract: Rising anthelmintic resistance in Haemonchus contortus and other gastrointestinal nematodes poses a critical challenge to livestock parasite management, underscoring the urgent need for novel therapeutic agents. This study evaluated the in vitro anthelmintic potential of green-synthesized silver nanoparticles (AgNPs) derived from Artemisia afra and Artemisia annua leaf extracts against adult worms. Aqueous leaf extracts were utilized to biosynthesize AgNPs by optimizing reaction parameters, including extract-to-silver nitrate ratio, concentration, pH, and incubation time. Phytochemical characterization identified alkaloids, coumarins, tannins, polyphenols, and saponins in both species, with A. afra demonstrating markedly higher total phenolic (282 mg GAE/g) and flavonoid (3655.56 mg QE/g) contents than A. annua. UV-Vis spectroscopy confirmed nanoparticle synthesis, exhibiting characteristic surface plasmon resonance peaks at 435 nm (A. afra-AgNPs) and 456 nm (A. annua-AgNPs). Anthelmintic efficacy was assessed using the Adult Worm Motility Assay across a concentration gradient (3-48 microg/mL) over 24 hours. Both AgNP formulations displayed dose-dependent inhibition of motility. Notably, A. afra-AgNPs exhibited superior potency, achieving lower IC50; values at 12 hours compared to A. annua-AgNPs and the commercial anthelmintic levamisole. At 48 microg/mL (12 hours), A. afra-AgNPs demonstrated significantly greater motility inhibition than A. annua-AgNPs, while surpassing levamisole at 12 microg/mL (18 hours). These findings highlight green-synthesized AgNPs from Artemisia species, particularly A. afra, as potent, eco-friendly nano-anthelmintic candidates, offering a sustainable approach to mitigate drug-resistant nematode infections in livestock.

papers.title: Parental death destabilizes wolf packs despite the benefits of larger pack size
papers.abstract: 1. Cooperative breeding is a fundamental feature of many animal family groups. However, few studies have quantified whether variation in group size meaningfully buffers social and reproductive consequences following parental death. 2. Using 17 years of data from a gray wolf (Canis lupus) population in Oregon, USA, we evaluated how parental death (the death of one or both parents) influenced pack dissolution, reproductive failure, and pup recruitment, and whether larger pack sizes mitigated these effects. 3. Across 303 pack-years, we recorded 69 parental deaths, 39 pack dissolutions, and 112 reproductive failures. Packs that experienced parental death were nearly five times more likely to dissolve (95% CI: 2.12-11.12), nearly 16 times more likely to fail reproductively (95% CI: 5.34-47.26), and recruited 66% fewer pups (95% CI: 49-78% fewer) than packs in which both parents survived. 4. Larger packs were associated with improved demographic outcomes overall, but these group-size benefits were insufficient to fully offset the elevated risks associated with parental death. 5. Our results show that numerous individuals can provide generalized pack-level demographic resilience but do not functionally replace parental roles, highlighting the importance of evaluating social structure in addition to population size. 6. By clarifying the limits of social buffering in a cooperatively breeding carnivore, this study advances understanding of how social systems respond to parental death.

papers.title: Cognition and brain gene expression vary with sex and body size in a polyphenic dung beetle (Onthophagus taurus)
papers.abstract: Individual variation in cognition can have critical fitness consequences for animals. Therefore, it is important to understand the relationship between cognition and ecologically relevant life history traits that vary within species. Furthermore, we lack a unified understanding of how these traits are integrated mechanistically with the cognitive outcomes they are associated with. We examined the relationship between cognitive performance on multiple tests on one side--and sex, a nutritionally-cued reproductive male polyphenism, and body size on the other--as well as their respective relationships to brain gene expression. Using the bull-headed dung beetle (Onthophagus taurus), we performed an associative learning assay, a spatial cognition assay, and a detour test on large fighter males, small sneaker males, and correspondingly large and small females. We then performed RNAseq on the brains of the beetles that had performed these assays. We found that sex was an important predictor of performance on the spatial cognition assay, while body size (which is closely related to early life nutrition) was associated with performance on the detour task. The associative learning assay did not yield significant results. RNAseq data revealed complex and multifaceted relationships between brain gene expression and our factors of interest. This work provides insights into the complex links between cognition, brains, and ecologically relevant traits.

papers.title: RePurpose: An LLM-Assisted, Source-Traceable Drug Repurposing Tool with Retrospective Validation on Clemastine in Multiple Sclerosis
papers.abstract: Summary Thus far, evidence for drug repurposing is contained in target-, drug-, trial-, and literature-based data sources that are challenging to synthesize for non-specialists. Here, we introduce RePurpose, a web-based tool that takes as input a topic written in plain language and returns candidate drugs built from data in Open Targets, ClinicalTrials.gov, UniProt, and PubMed. For queries in the form of a goal, RePurpose filters candidate drugs by whether they modulate all targets implicated in the goal in the corresponding direction. Every candidate has a source that contributes evidence: a structured database, a clinical trial, or a proposal from a large language model. An adjustable ranking adjusts the order of candidates from well-studied to less well-known candidate drugs. We retrospectively tested RePurpose with the trial drug clemastine, which was being considered as a remyelinating agent in multiple sclerosis (MS). RePurpose retrieved clemastine in each replicate of the mechanism-worded queries, but in no replicates of the disease-worded queries, and no structured query retrieved it without the language model enabled. Its ranked outputs reflected the evidence supporting clemastine but not later evidence of harm in progressive MS, which was reachable only through an on-demand literature search. Our results imply that RePurpose may be better at tracing evidence around a hypothesis than generating new hypotheses. Availability and Implementation RePurpose Pharma is freely accessible at https://www.repurposepharma.com/. For code and more information on the application, see: https://github.com/nayagamnitin-hub/RePurpose-Pharma.

papers.title: FEED, FLEE, OR FACT-FIND: MODELING LATENT COGNITIVE-MECHANISTIC RESPONSES TO HETEROSPECIFIC ALARM CALLS FOR FORAGING CARDINALS
papers.abstract: Heterospecific alarm calls allow animals to obtain information about predators from other species, but how receivers translate different forms of alarm information into defensive behavior remains poorly understood. In particular, signals may differ in whether they elicit rapid, relatively stereotyped responses or permit more graded evaluation of threat. We investigated this possibility by exposing foraging Northern cardinals (Cardinalis cardinalis) to playbacks of tufted titmouse (Baeolophus bicolor) calls associated with different predator contexts, including graded and immediate threats. To characterize responses, we developed a Bayesian latent-risk model that integrated three behaviors: feeding, vigilant looks, and departure, to estimate a shared dimension of perceived predation risk. Inferred risk increased from near-baseline levels under contact calls to intermediate levels under owl-associated call and the highest levels under ZZ calls. Increasing latent risk was associated with reduced expected seed intake and higher probability of complete feeding suppression. Vigilance showed a nonlinear relationship with inferred risk, increasing at intermediate levels before declining under the highest-risk treatment in favor of departure. This pattern is consistent with the possibility that receivers continue gathering information under intermediate threats but reduce vigilance when responding to more urgent danger. Although the experiment cannot fully establish whether these differences arise from canalized defensive responses or flexible cognitive evaluation, the results show how heterospecific alarm calls map onto distinct, coordinated behavioral responses.

papers.title: Evaluation and primer for using DeepLabCut to track small animals in large spaces
papers.abstract: DeepLabCut (DLC), a machine learning-based pose estimation tool, has dramatically increased the throughput of behavioral tracking. Yet its implication remains limited by lack of validation data from diverse scenarios and users' unfamiliarity with the machine learning workflow. Here, we provide a practical primer on DLC terminology and workflow and performance evaluation of DLC in a novel scenario where the target is much smaller than those in previous validation data. We assessed model performance in a total of 36 model configurations across three training proportions, six training iterations, and two recording resolutions. Performance was evaluated on training convergence, prediction error, prediction certainty, and generalizability. Additionally, we selected an optimal model based on a balance between model performance and training time and applied it to 20 recordings at each resolution. In the test frames, 15 and 6 out of 18 model configurations met all performance criteria under high- and low-resolution, respectively. Of these, DLC was able to achieve low prediction error, high prediction confidence, and low train-test loss. Prediction error and confidence varied with training proportion, iteration, and resolution. Inference using the optimal models achieved similar high confidence predictions, with low-likelihood predictions predominantly associated with visual obstruction, low light, and reduced contrast between the subject and the background. Notably, the optimal models for high- and low-resolutions performed similarly despite a multi-fold difference in the cost of the recording devices, providing validation data for DLC in low-budget research, teaching and outreach scenarios.

papers.title: Heatwaves and turbidity influxes have interacting and lasting effects on the foraging behaviour of three-spined stickleback Gasterosteus aculeatus
papers.abstract: Freshwater ecosystems support a disproportionately high share of fish species and biodiversity yet are among the most threatened ecosystems globally and are increasingly being exposed to multiple, co-occurring environmental stressors. In addition, predicting the combined impacts of environmental stressors remains a major challenge, particularly when stressors differ in how quickly they arise and how long their effects persist. Understanding how these stressors interact across time is critical for predicting their ecological consequences. Here, we examine how warming and turbidity, two widespread and intensifying stressors, interact to influence predator-prey dynamics in the three-spined stickleback (textit{Gasterosteus aculeatus}). Using a fully factorial experiment, fish were exposed to ambient, warmed, turbid, or combined conditions for short (one week) or prolonged (six weeks) periods, before feeding rates were quantified across prey densities using a novel stochastic Bayesian model. We found that foraging behaviour was shaped primarily by prior exposure rather than the immediate experimental conditions. Short-term exposure to both stressors increased feeding rates, whereas prolonged warming reduced them. In contrast, turbidity continued to increase feeding rates over both time periods and, when combined with warming, offset the negative effects of extended heat exposure. Changes in feeding performance at the individual level may propagate through food webs, potentially triggering trophic cascades that reduce biodiversity. Given the exceptional biodiversity of freshwater systems, such dynamics are of particular concern. We also found that behavioural changes persisted even after stressors were removed, indicating that exposure history can have lasting effects. These findings suggest that short-term experiments, such as the functional response, may actually be measuring subject experiential history rather than responses to specific experimental conditions.

papers.title: GAT1508, a selective neuronal GIRK1/2 activator, exhibits superior antiepileptic efficacy and synergizes with cannabidiol
papers.abstract: G protein-gated inwardly rectifying potassium (GIRK; Kir3) channels are key regulators of neuronal excitability and represent promising therapeutic targets for epilepsy. Here, we characterize GAT1508, a urea-based small-molecule activator selectively targeting neuronal GIRK1/2 heterotetramers, and compare its efficacy with previously described urea compounds ML297 and GiGA1. In a pentylenetetrazole (PTZ)-induced seizure model, GAT1508 demonstrated robust antiseizure activity, outperforming both ML297 and GiGA1 and achieving efficacy comparable to valproic acid. Electrophysiological studies using two-electrode voltage clamp in Xenopus oocytes revealed that GAT1508, unlike ML297 and GiGA1, selectively activates GIRK1/2 channels without significant activation of cardiac GIRK1/4 channels, suggesting reduced risk of cardiovascular side effects. Structural and computational analyses indicate that enhanced stabilization of GAT1508 compared to ML297 within the GIRK1/2 binding pocket promotes both ion permeation and channel gating through coordinated interactions with key residues. Furthermore, GAT1508, like the two other urea drugs, exhibited synergistic activation of GIRK channels when combined with G{beta}{gamma}-mediated pathways and significantly potentiated the antiseizure effects of cannabidiol (CBD) in both hippocampal slice recordings and in vivo seizure models. These findings establish GAT1508 as a potent and selective GIRK1/2 activator and support a novel combination therapeutic strategy for epilepsy based on convergent GIRK channel modulation.

papers.title: Disease progression shapes circadian and locomotor disruption in a model of multiple sclerosis
papers.abstract: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an autoimmune demyelinating disease of the central nervous system featuring a wide range of debilitating symptoms. Wearable activity recording devices have recently been adopted to improve symptom monitoring in MS, capturing symptoms related to sleep/wake cycles, circadian disruption, and fatigue. However, comparable measures of activity have yet been established in pre-clinical models of MS, the most widely used being experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE). We therefore sought to characterize changes in continual home-cage activity over the course of EAE, and establish whether home-cage monitoring can be used as an observer-independent measure of disease progression. Our results showed that locomotor activity in the mid-active/dark phase was most severely affected by EAE. Disrupted circadian (24-hour) activity was observed during the peak and onset stages of disease. Bout activity analysis revealed >40-minute long activity bouts as a sensitive indicator of non-motor symptoms independent of clinical score-based motor deficits. Current assessment of disease progression in EAE relies on clinical scores, which primarily assess motor deficits through visual observation prone to observer bias. Various computed activity parameters were found to be altered during key disease stages, suggesting that a combination of activity measures can serve as objective indicators of disease progression. Overall, our results show that home-cage activity effectively captures signs of non-motor symptoms in the EAE model of MS and can serve as an observer-independent measure of EAE disease progression.

papers.title: Aggregation dynamics of terrestrial isopods under extended Vicsek model
papers.abstract: Terrestrial isopods display a rich behavioral repertoire, including fast escape responses and aggregation dynamics. Their response to environmental stimuli such as artificial light, humidity, vibration, heat and predation stress has been documented, but research highlights a variability in these responses, depending on the studied species and the different ecological niches they inhabit. The Vicsek model is widely used in the study of collective behavior and has been adapted multiple times to model different biological phenomena. In this work, we exposed terrestrial isopod Porcellionides pruinosus to different combinations of vibration and light stimuli within a circular enclosure and used the resulting experimental observations to extend the Vicsek model to account for aggregation dynamics and speed variability. To this end, we modeled aggregation dynamics using local group size and edge proximity to modulate aggregation probability. Our experimental results suggest that the combined effect of light and vibration increases the speed of isopods more than light or vibration alone. Additionally, the speed relaxation also occurs later when exposed to the combined stimuli. Interestingly, the classic Vicsek model correctly predicted the motion of isopods only within a few seconds under stimuli presence, indicating the isopods move in a collective fashion at short time scales. In contrast, the results of simulating swarms with the extended Vicsek model were consistent with the mean square displacement of the experimentally tracked isopods over longer times and also, depending on the stimuli, for the short times. This extension of the Vicsek model provides a framework that can be used for multi-modal stimuli testing of terrestrial collective and aggregation invertebrate behavior, thus providing a platform to understand better the variability of the responses of these valuable members of the ecosystem.

papers.title: The anxiolytic-like effect of the aqueous extract of Punica granatum depends on the stress level of fish and mice: Evidence of a homeostatic re-establishing effect
papers.abstract: Pomegranate (Punica granatum) has shown potential anxiolytic and antidepressant effects in preclinical research, but its mechanisms remain unclear. Importantly, some evidence suggests that the effects of P. granatum depend on previous stress, suggesting an adaptogenic effect. This study aimed to evaluate the anxiolytic-like effects of an aqueous extract of P. granatum (AE-PG) on lambaris and zebrafish exposed to acute restraint stress (ARS) and female BALB/c mice exposed to unpredictable chronic mild stress (CUMS). In addition, we evaluated antidepressant-like effects in female BALB/c mice. Acute administration of AE-PG (1 mg/kg, i.p.) was tested in the novel tank test (NTT) in lambaris and zebrafish and in the light/dark test (LDT) in zebrafish, while chronic (7 days) administration of AE-PG (1 mg/kg, i.p.) was tested in the elevated plus-maze (EPM), open-field test (OFT), splash test (ST), and forced swim test (FST) in mice. ARS increased geotaxis and erratic swimming in the NTT, as well as scototaxis, risk assessment, and erratic swimming in the LDT. Acute pre-treatment with AE-PG blocked the effects of ARS on these anxiety-like endpoints in both lambaris and zebrafish. CUMS increased open arm avoidance in the EPM, thigmotaxis and horizontal and vertical exploration in the OFT, and immobility in the FST, and decreased grooming in the ST. Chronic treatment with AE-PG blocked the effects of CUMS on anxiety-like endpoints, and depression-like endpoints, in mice. An in silico analysis of the main compounds in AE-PG suggested a possible mechanism of action on a wide network of targets that converge on PI3K/Akt and show differential expression in brain regions associated with fear- and anxiety-like behavior. Molecular docking suggests that a compound from AE-PG, ellagic acid, is likely to act through estrogen receptors, which could help reestablish homeostatic balance in response to stress.

papers.title: Dopamine Release from the Locus Coeruleus Enables Temporal Binding in the Hippocampus
papers.abstract: The hippocampus forms memories by associating events that are separated in time. These associations can be studied using trace conditioning, a procedure where a temporal gap is inserted between a conditional stimulus and an unconditional stimulus. Here, we examined how dopaminergic projections to CA1 support trace fear conditioning. Using fiber photometry and genetic lesions, we demonstrate that locus coeruleus (LC)-derived dopamine, rather than VTA input, is the primary source of dopamine in CA1 and is essential for trace learning. LC lesions reduced CA1 principal neuron activity and c-Fos expression. In-vivo imaging revealed that successful learning requires post-shock reactivation of stimulus-specific ensembles, a process compromised by LC lesions or long trace intervals. Finally, optogenetic stimulation of LC-CA1 projections during the post-shock period was sufficient to rescue learning in long-trace protocols. These findings identify LC-CA1 dopamine as a critical regulator of temporal binding via the facilitation of hippocampal memory trace reactivation.

papers.title: A Structure-Based hERG Pose Selection Workflow Integrating Induced-Fit Docking, Shape Similarity, Interaction Fingerprints, and Molecular Dynamics
papers.abstract: The recent availability of several ligand-bound hERG/Kv11.1 cryo-EM structures creates an opportunity for prospective structure-based modeling, but it also introduces a practical problem: a new ligand may be compatible with only a subset of the available receptor conformations, and docking may generate several plausible poses within each template. We therefore evaluated a template-aware pose-selection framework using the astemizole-, pimozide-, and E4031-bound hERG structures as experimental reference environments, with apo 8ZYN included as a receptor-state control. The ligand set separated into two study-defined chemical regions: a low-polarity, highly lipophilic Group I represented by astemizole and pimozide, and a more polar Group II represented by E4031. Induced-fit docking (IFD) improved self-docking relative to rigid Glide, whereas apo 8ZYN did not reproduce ligand-bound behavior during short molecular dynamics (MD) assessment. Across the retrospective ligand-bound analyses, six of seven group-matched systems met the dual MD-quality criterion, whereas none of eight group-mismatched systems did. Highest static shape similarity was the most consistent pose-selection criterion for Group I, while an interaction-fingerprint (IFP)-favored 30:70 shape:IFP composite was retained provisionally for the single retrospective Group II reference. Application to dofetilide, ibutilide, and terfenadine produced binding hypotheses with residue-contact patterns consistent with independent hERG literature. Together, these results support using ligand-bound hERG structures as chemically selective reference environments for pose prioritization rather than as interchangeable receptor templates.

papers.title: The "glue-gun ant" Lordomyrma azumai uses an adhesive thread secretion to immobilize opponents
papers.abstract: In stinging Hymenoptera, the poison gland and its vesicle have been understood largely as sources of toxic, irritating, or antimicrobial compounds, which the sting injects into a target. However, external uses of poison gland secretions have also been reported: Pseudoneoponera (formerly Pachycondyla) froth a proteinaceous poison gland secretion into foam threads that entangle attacking ants, and Crematogaster smear opponents with a contact toxin generated on a spatulate sting from poison and Dufour gland products4. Here we report that workers of the myrmicine ant Lordomyrma azumai produce, in the poison vesicle, a secretion, likely proteinaceous, that solidifies upon extrusion into an adhesive thread. The sting is retained as the conduit, but the secretion it delivers is applied externally rather than injected, and acts as a structural material: workers wipe the thread onto opponents and tether them to the substrate. To our knowledge, no hymenopteran venom secretion functions as a solid thread; in the closest case, Pseudoneoponera3, the secretion entangles attackers as a foam rather than as a continuous solid filament.

papers.title: A Repulsive Bias in Perceived Heading Away from the Straight-Ahead as Determined by Continuous Psychophysics
papers.abstract: Previous studies of heading perception have reported both attraction toward and repulsion away from straight ahead. Different potential explanations for these differences have been brought forward, such as the reference frame of the response (where egocentric responses are connected to attraction and allocentric responses are connected to repulsion) or the response range (where a wider response range is related to more repulsion). In this study, we aimed to contribute to this debate using a novel Continuous Psychophysics-based task in virtual reality to investigate systematic heading biases across the full 360{degrees} range (repulsion predicted) in an egocentric task (attraction predicted), while concurrently examining the perceptual and motor contributions to these biases. Participants (n = 60 across two experiments) continuously indicated their perceived heading using a joystick while experiencing optic flow consistent with slow or fast self-motion while the simulated heading direction was changing continuously. In a CONTROL condition, participants aligned the joystick with the direction of a clearly visible arrow. The joystick was placed on the dominant-hand side in Experiment 1 (on the right for n = 28 participants) and in the middle and on the left in Experiment 2. In both experiments, we found consistent repulsion away from straight ahead in the CONTROL, FAST, and SLOW conditions, regardless of joystick position. Biases around the other cardinal directions were less consistent and generally tended to show attraction. Around straight ahead, we also observed a general progression from smaller biases in CONTROL to larger biases in FAST and SLOW, suggesting that decreased reliability of perceptual cues increased biases. The broad pattern of findings remained reasonably consistent across the three joystick positions. Our original prediction of attraction in an egocentric task was therefore not supported. Instead, the findings were more consistent with the response-range account, which links larger response ranges (like our 360{degrees} response range) to stronger repulsion. Our findings further support the use of Continuous Psychophysics to study systematic perceptual biases and provide a blueprint for the analytical steps required to do so.

papers.title: Current state of bioacoustics research of vocal repertoires
papers.abstract: Knowledge of the unique call types produced by a species has historically been an important part of ecological research. However, the definition of a call type is not straightforward, and across species and studies different methods are employed to study call types and vocal repertories. Here, we analysed the methodology used to identify the vocal repertoires of 197 mammalian species across 220 studies. We found a large variability in the features extract from individual calls, methods to analyse spectrographic features, and methods to cluster call types. We further see a low uptake of novel methods for acoustic analysis and clustering. Lastly, we identify a lack of open data across the included studies, with less than 2% of studies providing the raw audio dataset underlying their paper. Based on these results, we call for increased standardization of methods and data transparency across the field.

papers.title: Stochastic Decision Policy Is Optimal Under Costly Control
papers.abstract: Human and animal decisions are often noisy. This variability is usually attributed to noise that corrupts the decision evidence, a defect that an ideal decision maker would eliminate. Here we ask whether stochastic choice can instead be optimal once the cost of implementing prescribed policies is counted. We treat the decision maker as an ideal observer that maximizes expected gain but pays costs to sharpen its policy away from a random default. Using sequential sampling, a setting in which the optimal policy is precisely defined, we show that this trade-off makes a stochastic policy optimal, replacing the hard decision boundaries of classical theory with soft stopping zones whose softness is set by the price of control. This soft policy aligns with the strategy used in cutting-edge artificial learning agents for robustness. Noise that corrupts the agent's belief, an important confound of noisy behavior, produces superficially similar yet distinctive signatures in behavioral policies. Leveraging this, we recovered the policies of two macaques with low-dimensional recurrent neural networks and found that their behavior carries both a stochastic policy and belief noise. By separating variability in constructing a decision belief from stochasticity in selecting actions, these results establish that stochastic decision policies can themselves be optimal, offering a common principle for understanding behavioral variability in biological and artificial decision makers.

papers.title: LNP Delivery of Prime Editors Enables Durable Correction of PAH R408W in Phenylketonuria Models
papers.abstract: Phenylketonuria (PKU) is a monogenic metabolic disorder caused by mutations in the phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH) gene, the most common of which is c.1222C>T (p.R408W). Current treatment options, including dietary restriction and enzyme substitution, can be effective but are often challenging for patients to maintain and do not address the underlying genetic defect. Gene editing represents a compelling one-time treatment approach for PKU. Herein, we demonstrate mRNA:LNP-mediated delivery of prime editors that enable therapeutically-relevant levels of correction of the R408W mutation in both in vitro and in vivo model systems. Further, we found that co-delivery of the DNA repair modulator RAD18 and engineering of the prime editor protein, enabled 2-fold and 3-fold increases in prime editing relative to PE3 respectively, resulting in ~50% correction efficiency in a humanized PKU mouse model. Collectively, this work identifies novel potential approaches to enhancing prime editing and establishes LNP-delivered prime editing as a mutation-specific, non-viral therapeutic strategy for PKU, as well as providing a framework for extending prime editing to other inherited liver diseases.

papers.title: Sparse Phosphorylatable Residues, Tuned by Agonist Chemotype, Shapes GPCR Signaling
papers.abstract: GPCR signaling diversity is often attributed to an intracellular phosphorylation barcode, in which ligand-dependent modification of multiple receptor phosphoresidues encodes selective engagement of downstream transducers. However, whether such an extensive phosphorylation of the receptor is universally required remains unclear. Here, we show that the melanocortin-4 receptor (MC4R), a central regulator of energy homeostasis, achieves remarkably diverse and pathway-selective signaling through a sparse set of strategically positioned regulatory phosphoresidues. Systematic study of these phosphoresidues within helix 8 and the C-terminal tail revealed distinct, spatially segregated contributions to receptor function. Substitution of helix 8 residues S306 disrupted beta arrestin2 recruitment, early endosomal trafficking, and ERK1/2 activation, while visibly altering G alpha-cAMP signaling in all the receptor variants. In contrast, distal C-terminal substitutions had little effect on beta-arrestin2 coupling and trafficking, revealing that these regions are not functionally redundant. Surprisingly, signaling through G alpha q/11- and G alpha12/13-linked pathways remained largely constrained across receptor variants, further demonstrating pathway-specific control by these phosphoresidues. Notably, ligand chemotype reshaped the functional consequences of these substitutions: setmelanotide selectively restored or enhanced signaling through pathways that were compromised by specific receptor mutations. Together, our findings argue that GPCR signaling diversity does not necessarily require an extensive phosphorylation barcode. Instead, MC4R uses a minimal number of spatially organized phosphoresidue that can differentially control transducer engagement and downstream signaling, while ligand chemistry determines how this regulatory landscape is accessed.

papers.title: How social value guides curiosity, information search, and memory in younger and older adults
papers.abstract: Epistemic curiosity, or the desire for new knowledge, benefits emotional, physical, and cognitive health across the lifespan. Initially believed to be solely intrinsically motivated, recent work has found that extrinsic motivators can also drive epistemic curiosity. One example of the latter is the perceived social value of information, such as popularity metrics on social media platforms (e.g., upvotes on Reddit.com). However, it remains unclear whether the influence of social value cues extends to curiosity-related behaviors, such as information search and memory, and whether these effects vary with age. The current study was designed to fill these knowledge gaps. In two experiments, younger and older adults (total N = 367) rated their curiosity for user-generated trivia questions that varied in social value (high or low upvote counts on Reddit.com). Upvote counts were either visible (upvote visible condition) or not visible (upvote invisible condition). In Experiment 1, participants had the opportunity to reveal the answer to each trivia question, a measure of information seeking. Although social value increased curiosity, it did not influence information seeking. In Experiment 2, answer reveal was mandatory, and participants received a surprise recall test for the answers. Social value again increased curiosity, particularly for younger adults, but had no influence on memory. Overall, these findings replicate social-value effects on curiosity in younger and older adults, but they provide no evidence that social value motivates information search or episodic memory. These findings highlight the limits of extrinsic influences on epistemic behaviors across the adult lifespan.

papers.title: The Impact of Small-group Education on Student Wellbeing in Undergraduate Biology: a Student Perspective on Self-Determination Theory
papers.abstract: Alarming reports about mental health have raised awareness of student wellbeing in STEM Education. Self-Determination Theory (SDT) implies that wellbeing can be improved by fulfilling the needs for autonomy, competence and relatedness. Educational design elements such as small-group teaching, peer feedback and offering a low-stakes practice environment can help fulfill these SDT needs. These elements were applied in a new academic skills course in our undergraduate Biology program. Here, we investigated how this affected the students sense of autonomy, competence and relatedness, and whether this was related to wellbeing. First, a survey among 48 students confirmed that student wellbeing is positively correlated to SDT fulfillment. Next, group interviews with students revealed that wellbeing is mostly dependent on relatedness, which is facilitated through small-group teaching in the first semester. Furthermore, students reported that (1) relatedness evolves through bonding with peers over the shared experience of struggle, (2) competence requires (peer) feedback and opportunities for growth, especially in laboratory coursework and (3) a structured, low-stakes environment supports competence, but without optimal challenge, also undermines a sense of autonomy. This illustrates how students perceive the effects of small-group educational activities on their wellbeing through the lens of Self-Determination Theory.

papers.title: Evidence for a cohesion-related function of alpaca hums: Linking automated call detection with GPS data
papers.abstract: Understanding how animals communicate while moving helps explain social dynamics, but simultaneously tracking vocal and spatial behaviour in freely moving groups remains challenging. Animal-borne audio and GPS recordings can place naturally occurring vocalisations in their spatial context, but continuous recordings generate large datasets that require automated call detection.We used this approach to investigate whether alpaca hums, a poorly characterised vocalisation, contribute to group cohesion. We combined automated detection of hums from continuous collar-borne audio with synchronised GPS data from a partially collared herd to test whether humming is associated with changes in spacing and movement consistent with a contact-call function. We combined deep-learning-assisted detection with manual validation to build a large curated hum corpus from 2,011 h of continuous recordings from a partially collared herd. We then tested how humming was associated with spacing and movement at both individual and group levels. Following hum production, distance between focal alpaca and the group shifted toward closer contact relative to matched non-hum periods. Hums were also more likely to occur when the collared alpaca moved faster. These findings support a cohesion-related role of hums and suggest that this call type may help alpaca maintain social contact while moving. More broadly, our study shows how automated call detection combined with movement data can place poorly characterised vocalisations in a behavioural context, narrow their plausible functions, and generate targeted hypotheses even when caller identity remains uncertain and only part of a group can be collared. This approach extends functional research on vocal communication to species whose calls remain poorly understood.

papers.title: Risk management strategies in social grooming among Tonkean and rhesus macaques
papers.abstract: Group-living individuals interact constantly, maintaining cohesion, stability, and security within their social groups. However, these interactions can entail risks that individuals must manage to optimize their social navigation through complex social groups, such as those of non-human primates. Here, we investigated how macaques manage risk during social grooming by analysing its somatic modalities, including body orientation and body site being groomed. We compared two macaque species with contrasting social styles: the more despotic rhesus macaque and the more tolerant Tonkean macaque. Using dyadic analyses including species, kinship, age difference, rank difference, and male presence as predictors, we found marked species differences in grooming patterns. Tonkean macaques engaged more frequently in face-to-face grooming and less in face-to-back grooming compared to rhesus macaques. They also groomed body sites associated with high eye-contact probability, such as the head, neck, and chest, more often than rhesus macaques. Kin dyads groomed these body sites more often, particularly in rhesus macaques. These findings suggest that avoiding body sites associated with potential eye-contact may constitute a risk management strategy during grooming. Overall, our results reveal a previously overlooked dimension of primate social cognition that may shape dyadic relationships and social network structure.

papers.title: The effect of dominance rank on behavioural response to playback calls in ring-tailed lemurs (Lemur catta)
papers.abstract: In group-living species, dominance hierarchies play a central role in shaping social dynamics, influencing both agonistic and affiliative interactions. Being able to recognise an individual's dominance rank at a distance, can reduce direct conflicts, facilitating group coordination, and mediating social cohesion. While the role of dominance in relation to aggressive or reproductive vocalizations has been well documented, its influence on affiliative contact calls, particularly in mediating group movement and social integration, remains underexplored. We conducted playback experiments with free-ranging adult ringtailed lemurs (Lemur catta) at the Affenwald Wildlife Park to investigate how dominance rank of the caller and rank differences between caller and listener affect behavioral responses. Using Generalized Linear Mixed Models (GLMMs), we analysed three response variables: vocal response, number of visual scans, and occurrence of movement. Our results revealed sex-specific effects: females exhibited increased movement following contact calls from high-ranking individuals, and tended to refrain from moving when their own rank exceeded that of the caller. In contrast, no significant effects of dominance rank were observed in males. These findings suggest that high-ranking females may play an important role in initiating group movement. This study provides insights into the role of dominance rank in mediating social coordination through contact calls and provides a foundation for further research into the role of vocal communication in maintaining group cohesion in primates.

papers.title: Percussive manipulations distinguish object play in capuchin and patas monkeys
papers.abstract: Object play has been proposed as a developmental precursor of flexible tool use. We applied a standardized object play protocol, previously used with corvids and parrots, to tufted capuchin monkeys (Sapajus apella), a member of a genus known for tool use, and patas monkeys (Erythrocebus patas), for which tool use has not been reported. Both groups were tested in a zoo across 15 sessions with a standardized set of objects and activity plates. All capuchins smashed objects, whereas only two patas monkeys did so, a difference consistent with the per-cussive foraging of capuchins. The species did not differ significantly in behavioral variability, object combinations, manipulation time, number of body parts used, or tail use, and combination rates were low in both. The species thus differed in a specific form of manipulation rather than in overall or combinatory object play. With one species per category and small samples, these results cannot establish whether combinatory object play is associated with tool use in primates.
